the recombinant O. oeni and L. brevis enzymes have different pH and temperature optima and that the O. oeni enzyme has higher specific activity and is more stable at high temperatures than the L. brevis enzyme.

we have characterized three new family 51 α-l-arabinosidases from two lactic acid bacteria and that the recombinant α-l-arabinose degrading enzymes of Oenocococus oeni and L. brevis are more efficient than the commercial enzyme of A. niger.

the recombinant family 51 arabino-furanosidases were able to hydrolyze the non-reducing terminal residues of the arabinan side chains of arabinan, arabinoxylan, and arabinogalactan, but they did not hydrolyze the arabinofuranosyl linkages in arabinose-containing oligosaccharides or in arabinan.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the heterologous expression of two putative α-l-arabofuranosidase genes from Oenococcocus oeni and L. brevis, and the subsequent characterization of the resulting recombinant enzymes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the O. oeni and L. brevis arabinosidases are not suitable as a replacement of the A. niger arabinosid-ase.
the O. oeni α-l-arabinosidase is the most active and most thermostable enzyme among the three enzymes tested.

the enzymes of O. oeni and L. brevis are highly specific for the hydrolysis of α-l-arabinose residues in arabinans and that they are not able to degrade the backbone of the polysaccharide, as shown for A. niger arabinosidases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
both enzymes have a similar substrate specificity, but the O. oeni enzyme has a higher affinity to the substrate and is more active.

the recombinant O. oeni α-l-arabinosidase was the most efficient in hydrolyzing α-l-arabinopyranosides, while the recombinant A. niger and L. brevis α-l-arabinohydrolases were most active on α-l-arabinooligosaccharides.
the recombinant family 51 α-l-arabinosidases of Lb. brevis (LbABF1) and Oe. oeni (OeABF1) are both able to degrade arabinan and arabinoxylan.
The main takeaway from our work is that
these enzymes have different substrate specificities, which is likely due to their different substrate-binding clefts.
O. oeni and L. brevis family 51 α-l-arabinosidases are active on p-nitrophenyl α-l-arabinopyranoside and arabinan, but not on arabinooligosaccharides.
O. oeni Araf51 and LbAraf51 have different substrate preferences and are more active on arabinans of low DP than the Aspergillus enzyme.
